records.source: אַחַ֣ר׀הַדְּבָרִ֣ים הָאֵ֗לֶּה גִּדַּל֩ הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֜וֹשׁ אֶת־הָמָ֧ן בֶּֽן־הַמְּדָ֛תָא הָאֲגָגִ֖י וַֽיְנַשְּׂאֵ֑הוּ וַיָּ֨שֶׂם֙ אֶת־כִּסְא֔וֹ מֵעַ֕ל כָּל־הַשָּׂרִ֖ים אֲשֶׁ֥ר אִתּֽוֹ׃
records.gloss: After the things the these made great the king Ahasuerus Haman son [of] Hammedatha the Agagite, and lifted him up, and set his seat from above all the princes who [were] with him.
pieces: Some time later King Ahasuerus promoted Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite. He raised him high and gave him a seat above all the officials who served with him.

L.1: After these things King Ahasuerus made Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite great, and he lifted him up and set his seat above all the princes who were with him.

R.1: Some time later, King Ahasuerus gave Haman son of Hammedatha a high position. Haman was an Agagite. The king honored him and gave him a place above all the other leaders around him.

decisions.choice: the Agagite: a descendant of Agag, the king of Amalek, as the story invites the reader to hear
alternatives: a man from an otherwise unknown place or clan called Agag
decisions.reason: Agag was the king of Amalek whom Saul spared against the LORD's command (1 Samuel 15:8-33), and Amalek was Israel's old enemy (Exodus 17:8-16; Deuteronomy 25:17-19). Mordecai is introduced as a Benjaminite, a descendant of Kish (2:5), the family of Saul (1 Samuel 9:1-2). So the quarrel between Haman and Mordecai echoes the old one between Saul and Agag. The text does not say that Haman descends from that Agag; it lets the names speak, and no other people called Agagites is known.

decisions.choice: made great, lifted up, set his seat above: promoted him to the highest rank at court
decisions.reason: Three verbs pile up the honor. A seat set above the other officials is a place of rank at the king's side (compare 1 Kings 2:19; 2 Kings 25:28). The reader has just learned that Mordecai saved the king's life and was not rewarded (2:21-23); the man promoted is someone else.

decisions.choice: after these things: some time after the events of chapter 2
decisions.reason: The phrase marks a new episode without saying how long after. Esther became queen in the king's seventh year (2:16), and the lot is cast in his twelfth year (3:7), so some years may lie between.

decisions.choice: princes (Literal); officials (Balanced); leaders (Readable)
decisions.reason: The word for the king's high officers is rendered as in the books before (princes, officials, leaders), so that Literal keeps the old word and Balanced and Readable say what these men were.

records.heading: Haman seeks to annihilate the Jews

records.source: וְכָל־עַבְדֵ֨י הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ אֲשֶׁר־בְּשַׁ֣עַר הַמֶּ֗לֶךְ כֹּרְעִ֤ים וּמִֽשְׁתַּחֲוִים֙ לְהָמָ֔ן כִּי־כֵ֖ן צִוָּה־ל֣וֹ הַמֶּ֑לֶךְ וּמָ֨רְדֳּכַ֔י לֹ֥א יִכְרַ֖ע וְלֹ֥א יִֽשְׁתַּחֲוֶֽה׃
records.gloss: And all [the] servants of the king who [were] in [the] gate of the king [were] kneeling and bowing down to Haman, for so had commanded concerning him the king; and Mordecai would not kneel and would not bow down.
pieces: All the king's officials at the king's gate used to kneel and bow down to Haman, because the king had ordered it for him. But Mordecai would not kneel or bow down.

L.2: And all the servants of the king who were in the gate of the king were kneeling and bowing down to Haman, for so the king had commanded concerning him. But Mordecai would not kneel and would not bow down.

R.2: All the king's officials who worked at the palace gate knelt and bowed low to Haman, because the king had ordered them to do this. But Mordecai would not kneel or bow down to him.

decisions.choice: the king's gate: the palace entrance where royal officials sat and served
decisions.reason: In the ancient Near East the gate of a city or palace was where business was done and officials sat. Mordecai "sat in the king's gate" (2:19, 21), so he was one of these officials and had to pass Haman daily.

decisions.choice: Mordecai would not kneel or bow down: the text gives no reason beyond his being a Jew
alternatives: he refused to give a man honor due to God alone
he refused because Haman was an Amalekite
decisions.reason: Bowing to kings and officials was ordinary courtesy in Israel too (2 Samuel 14:4; 1 Kings 1:16), so the refusal is not simply a rule against bowing. The only explanation the text gives is that Mordecai told them he was a Jew (verse 4). Readers have suggested that he would not honor a man as divine, or that he would not bow to a descendant of Agag (see verse 1); the story leaves it open.

decisions.choice: were kneeling ... would not kneel: a repeated, ongoing action
decisions.reason: The participles describe what the officials kept doing, and the verbs for Mordecai describe a continuing refusal, day after day (verse 4), not a single incident.

decisions.choice: servants (Literal); officials (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: The king's servants here are his court officials, so Balanced and Readable say "officials", as with the king's servants elsewhere in these books.

records.source: וַיֹּ֨אמְר֜וּ עַבְדֵ֥י הַמֶּ֛לֶךְ אֲשֶׁר־בְּשַׁ֥עַר הַמֶּ֖לֶךְ לְמָרְדֳּכָ֑י מַדּ֨וּעַ֙ אַתָּ֣ה עוֹבֵ֔ר אֵ֖ת מִצְוַ֥ת הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃
records.gloss: And said [the] servants of the king who [were] in [the] gate of the king to Mordecai, Why [are] you transgressing the commandment of the king?
pieces: Then the king's officials at the king's gate said to Mordecai, "Why do you disobey the king's command?"

L.3: And the servants of the king who were in the gate of the king said to Mordecai, "Why are you transgressing the commandment of the king?"

R.3: The king's officials at the palace gate asked Mordecai, "Why are you disobeying the king's order?"

decisions.choice: transgressing the commandment of the king: crossing over, breaking a royal order
decisions.reason: The verb means "pass over" or "cross" and is used of breaking a command (Numbers 14:41; 1 Samuel 15:24). Here the command is the king's order to honor Haman (verse 2).

decisions.choice: disobey (Balanced, Readable)
decisions.reason: "Transgress" is kept at Literal to show the Hebrew picture of crossing a line; "disobey" says the same in plain words.

records.source: וַיְהִ֗י כְּאָמְרָ֤ם אֵלָיו֙ י֣וֹם וָי֔וֹם וְלֹ֥א שָׁמַ֖ע אֲלֵיהֶ֑ם וַיַּגִּ֣ידוּ לְהָמָ֗ן לִרְאוֹת֙ הֲיַֽעַמְדוּ֙ דִּבְרֵ֣י מָרְדֳּכַ֔י כִּֽי־הִגִּ֥יד לָהֶ֖ם אֲשֶׁר־ה֥וּא יְהוּדִֽי׃
records.gloss: And it was, as they spoke to him day and day, and he did not listen to them, and they told Haman, to see whether would stand [the] words of Mordecai, for he had told them that he [was] a Jew.
pieces: Day after day they spoke to him, but he would not listen to them. So they told Haman, to see whether Mordecai's reason would be accepted, since he had told them that he was a Jew.

L.4: And it came about, when they spoke to him day after day and he did not listen to them, that they told Haman, to see whether the words of Mordecai would stand, for he had told them that he was a Jew.

R.4: They talked to him about it every day, but he would not listen. So they told Haman about it. They wanted to see if Mordecai's excuse would be accepted, because he had told them that he was a Jew.

decisions.choice: as they spoke: the written and the read text differ by one letter
decisions.reason: The consonants written in the Hebrew text say "when they spoke" and the marginal reading says "as they spoke"; the two prepositions differ by one similar letter, and either way the sense is the same. The source data follows the marginal reading.

decisions.choice: whether the words of Mordecai would stand: whether his explanation would hold good
alternatives: whether Mordecai would stand firm in what he said
decisions.reason: To "stand" is used of words that hold or are accepted (Isaiah 40:8). The officials want to see whether being a Jew would excuse him from the king's command. Mordecai's "words" are his stated reason, given in the last clause.

decisions.choice: he had told them that he was a Jew
decisions.reason: Mordecai had told Esther to keep her people secret (2:10, 20), yet he makes his own known. It is this fact, more than the refusal itself, that turns Haman's anger against a whole people (verse 6).

decisions.choice: his reason (Balanced); excuse (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "words" means here, the reason he gave; Literal keeps "words".

records.source: וַיַּ֣רְא הָמָ֔ן כִּי־אֵ֣ין מָרְדֳּכַ֔י כֹּרֵ֥עַ וּמִֽשְׁתַּחֲוֶ֖ה ל֑וֹ וַיִּמָּלֵ֥א הָמָ֖ן חֵמָֽה׃
records.gloss: And saw Haman that not Mordecai [was] kneeling and bowing down to him, and was filled Haman [with] rage.
pieces: When Haman saw that Mordecai did not kneel or bow down to him, he was filled with rage.

L.5: And Haman saw that Mordecai was not kneeling and bowing down to him, and Haman was filled with rage.

R.5: When Haman saw for himself that Mordecai would not kneel or bow down to him, he was furious.

decisions.choice: rage: burning anger
decisions.reason: The word is used of hot, fierce anger, the same word used of the king's anger in 1:12 and 7:7, and of Haman again in 5:9.

decisions.choice: saw for himself
decisions.reason: Haman had heard about it from the officials (verse 4); now he sees it. Readable adds "for himself" to make that step clear.

records.source: וַיִּ֣בֶז בְּעֵינָ֗יו לִשְׁלֹ֤חיָד֙ בְּמָרְדֳּכַ֣י לְבַדּ֔וֹ כִּֽי־הִגִּ֥ידוּ ל֖וֹ אֶת־עַ֣ם מָרְדֳּכָ֑י וַיְבַקֵּ֣שׁ הָמָ֗ן לְהַשְׁמִ֧יד אֶת־כָּל־הַיְּהוּדִ֛ים אֲשֶׁ֛ר בְּכָל־מַלְכ֥וּת אֲחַשְׁוֵר֖וֹשׁ עַ֥ם מָרְדֳּכָֽי׃
records.gloss: And it was contemptible in his eyes to stretch out a hand on Mordecai by himself, for they had told him the people of Mordecai; and sought Haman to annihilate all the Jews who [were] in all [the] kingdom of Ahasuerus, [the] people of Mordecai.
pieces: But he thought it beneath him to lay hands on Mordecai alone, since they had told him who Mordecai's people were. So Haman looked for a way to wipe out all the Jews throughout the kingdom of Ahasuerus, Mordecai's people.

L.6: But it was contemptible in his eyes to lay a hand on Mordecai alone, for they had told him the people of Mordecai. And Haman sought to annihilate all the Jews who were in the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus, the people of Mordecai.

R.6: But he thought it was not enough to kill only Mordecai. They had told him what people Mordecai belonged to. So Haman made plans to destroy all the Jews in the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus, all of Mordecai's people.

decisions.choice: it was contemptible in his eyes: he scorned to do only this
decisions.reason: Literally "he despised in his eyes". Taking revenge on one man seemed too small to Haman; his pride wanted a larger target. "Lay a hand on" means to harm or kill (2:21).

decisions.choice: annihilate: destroy completely, wipe out
decisions.reason: The verb means to exterminate a people (Deuteronomy 9:3; 2 Samuel 21:5). It is the first of the three verbs in the decree (3:13; 7:4).

decisions.choice: the people of Mordecai: said twice, framing Haman's plan
decisions.reason: The phrase stands in the middle and again at the end of the verse. Haman's hatred moves from one man to his whole people, and the repetition makes that plain.

decisions.choice: thought it was not enough
decisions.reason: Readable says what the idiom means for Haman, that killing one man was too little for him.

records.source: בַּחֹ֤דֶשׁ הָרִאשׁוֹן֙ הוּא־חֹ֣דֶשׁ נִיסָ֔ן בִּשְׁנַת֙ שְׁתֵּ֣ים עֶשְׂרֵ֔ה לַמֶּ֖לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֑וֹשׁ הִפִּ֣יל פּוּר֩ ה֨וּא הַגּוֹרָ֜ל לִפְנֵ֣י הָמָ֗ן מִיּ֧וֹם׀לְי֛וֹם וּמֵחֹ֛דֶשׁ לְחֹ֥דֶשׁ שְׁנֵים־עָשָׂ֖ר הוּא־חֹ֥דֶשׁ אֲדָֽר׃ס
records.gloss: In the month the first, that [is the] month [of] Nisan, in [the] year twelve of the king Ahasuerus, [one] cast Pur, that [is] the lot, before Haman from day to day and from month to month, twelve, that [is the] month [of] Adar.
pieces: In the first month, which is the month Nisan, in the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus, they cast Pur, that is, the lot, in front of Haman, day by day and month by month, and it fell on the twelfth month, which is the month Adar.

L.7: In the first month, which is the month Nisan, in the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus, Pur, that is the lot, was cast before Haman, from day to day and from month to month, to the twelfth month, which is the month Adar.

R.7: In the first month of the year, the month of Nisan, in the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus, they threw Pur, that is, the lot, in front of Haman. They did this to choose a day and a month. The lot fell on the twelfth month, the month of Adar.

decisions.choice: Pur, that is, the lot: a foreign word, explained by the Hebrew one
decisions.reason: Pur is a word from the language of Mesopotamia for a lot, such as a marked stone or die; the writer explains it with the ordinary Hebrew word for lot. The feast of Purim takes its name from it (9:24-26).

decisions.choice: from day to day and from month to month, twelve: the lot was cast for each day and month until it chose the twelfth month
alternatives: the casting itself went on day after day for months
decisions.reason: The Hebrew is brief and leaves out a verb before "twelve". The most natural reading is that the lot was cast to choose a lucky day and month, and it fell on Adar. The day, the thirteenth, is given in verse 13.

decisions.choice: the first month, Nisan, and the twelfth, Adar; the twelfth year
decisions.reason: Nisan falls in March-April and Adar in February-March, so the lot set the date almost a year ahead. The twelfth year of Ahasuerus (Xerxes) is about 474 BC. The writer uses the Babylonian month names that Jews used after the exile (Nehemiah 2:1).

decisions.choice: and it fell on (Balanced); The lot fell on (Readable)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable supply the verb the Hebrew leaves out, so that "the twelfth month" reads as the result of the lot.

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר הָמָן֙ לַמֶּ֣לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵר֔וֹשׁ יֶשְׁנ֣וֹ עַם־אֶחָ֗ד מְפֻזָּ֤ר וּמְפֹרָד֙ בֵּ֣ין הָֽעַמִּ֔ים בְּכֹ֖ל מְדִינ֣וֹת מַלְכוּתֶ֑ךָ וְדָתֵיהֶ֞ם שֹׁנ֣וֹת מִכָּל־עָ֗ם וְאֶת־דָּתֵ֤י הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ אֵינָ֣ם עֹשִׂ֔ים וְלַמֶּ֥לֶךְ אֵין־שֹׁוֶ֖ה לְהַנִּיחָֽם׃
records.gloss: And said Haman to the king Ahasuerus, There is a people one scattered and separated among the peoples in all [the] provinces of your kingdom, and their laws [are] different from every people, and the laws of the king they [are] not doing, and for the king not [is] fitting to leave them.
pieces: Then Haman said to King Ahasuerus, "There is a certain people scattered and kept apart among the peoples in all the provinces of your kingdom. Their laws are different from those of every other people, and they do not keep the king's laws. It does the king no good to tolerate them.

L.8: And Haman said to King Ahasuerus, "There is one people scattered and separated among the peoples in all the provinces of your kingdom, and their laws are different from those of every people, and they do not keep the laws of the king, and it is not fitting for the king to leave them alone.

R.8: Then Haman said to King Ahasuerus, "There is a group of people spread out among the other peoples in every province of your kingdom. They keep themselves separate. Their laws are different from everyone else's, and they do not obey the king's laws. It is not in your best interest to let them go on like this.

decisions.choice: one people: Haman does not name them
decisions.reason: Haman speaks of "a people" without saying who they are, and the king does not ask (verses 10-11). The king learns who they are only when Esther tells him (7:3-6).

decisions.choice: scattered and separated: spread among the nations and keeping apart from them
decisions.reason: The first word means scattered abroad; the second can mean dispersed, or separated, kept distinct. The next clause, about their different laws, suggests the second sense: they live everywhere but stay a people apart.

decisions.choice: laws: the customs and rules of a people, and the king's decrees
decisions.reason: The word for law is the Persian loanword used throughout Esther for royal decrees (1:19; 3:14). Haman uses it for the Jews' way of life and for the king's laws in the same breath. His charge that they do not keep the king's laws rests on Mordecai's one refusal (verses 2-4).

decisions.choice: not fitting to leave them: not worth the king's while to let them be
decisions.reason: The verb means to be equal to or worth something (5:13; 7:4). Haman argues that tolerating them brings the king no profit, and offers money in the next verse.

decisions.choice: does the king no good to tolerate them
alternatives: it is not appropriate for the king to leave them alone
decisions.reason: Balanced brings out the sense of profit in the verb, which the next verse makes plain.

records.source: אִם־עַל־הַמֶּ֣לֶךְ ט֔וֹב יִכָּתֵ֖ב לְאַבְּדָ֑ם וַעֲשֶׂ֨רֶת אֲלָפִ֜ים כִּכַּר־כֶּ֗סֶף אֶשְׁקוֹל֙ עַל־יְדֵי֙ עֹשֵׂ֣י הַמְּלָאכָ֔ה לְהָבִ֖יא אֶל־גִּנְזֵ֥י הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃
records.gloss: If on the king [it is] good, let it be written to destroy them, and ten thousand talents [of] silver I will weigh out on [the] hands of [the] doers of the work, to bring into [the] treasuries of the king.
pieces: If it pleases the king, let a decree be written to destroy them, and I will pay {{units:about 375 tons of silver|ten thousand talents of silver}} into the hands of the officials in charge of the king's business, to be put into the royal treasuries."

L.9: If it is good to the king, let it be written that they be destroyed, and I will weigh out ten thousand talents of silver into the hands of those who do the work, to bring into the treasuries of the king."

R.9: If the king agrees, let an order be written to destroy them. I will pay {{units:about 375 tons of silver|ten thousand talents of silver}} to the officials who handle the king's business, to be put in the king's treasury."

decisions.choice: if it is good to the king: the court's polite formula for a request
decisions.reason: The same formula introduces requests to the king throughout the book (1:19; 5:4; 7:3; 8:5). It means "if the king approves".

decisions.choice: ten thousand talents of silver: an enormous sum
decisions.reason: A talent was about 75 pounds of silver, so the sum is about 375 tons. Herodotus (Histories 3.95) gives the yearly tribute of the whole Persian empire as under fifteen thousand talents of silver, so Haman offers a large part of an empire's yearly income. Whether he means it literally or as a grand gesture, the text does not say.

decisions.choice: those who do the work: the officials in charge of the king's business
alternatives: the men who carry out the killing
decisions.reason: The same phrase is used of royal officials in 9:3, where "those who do the king's work" are listed with the satraps and governors. Here they receive the silver and bring it into the treasury.

decisions.choice: about 375 tons of silver, with ten thousand talents of silver as the alternative
decisions.reason: Literal keeps the talent; Balanced and Readable give the modern weight with the original unit as a reader setting, as elsewhere for money and weights.

decisions.choice: If it pleases the king (Balanced); If the king agrees (Readable)
alternatives: If it is good to the king
decisions.reason: The idiom is put in natural English; Literal keeps the Hebrew wording.

records.source: וַיָּ֧סַר הַמֶּ֛לֶךְ אֶת־טַבַּעְתּ֖וֹ מֵעַ֣ל יָד֑וֹ וַֽיִּתְּנָ֗הּ לְהָמָ֧ן בֶּֽן־הַמְּדָ֛תָא הָאֲגָגִ֖י צֹרֵ֥ר הַיְּהוּדִֽים׃
records.gloss: And removed the king his signet ring from on his hand, and gave it to Haman son [of] Hammedatha the Agagite, [the] enemy of the Jews.
pieces: So the king took his signet ring off his hand and gave it to Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the enemy of the Jews.

L.10: And the king took his signet ring from his hand and gave it to Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the enemy of the Jews.

R.10: So the king took off his signet ring and gave it to Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the enemy of the Jews. With it Haman could seal orders in the king's name.

decisions.choice: the signet ring: the king's seal, which gave a document his authority
decisions.reason: A document pressed with the king's seal carried the king's own authority (verse 12; 8:8, 10). Giving the ring to Haman lets him issue laws in the king's name; later the same ring passes to Mordecai (8:2). Pharaoh did the same for Joseph (Genesis 41:42).

decisions.choice: the enemy of the Jews: one who harasses and attacks them
decisions.reason: The word means one who shows hostility, an adversary. The book gives Haman this title again (8:1; 9:10, 24), now at the moment he receives power to act on it.

decisions.choice: With it Haman could seal orders in the king's name.
decisions.reason: Readable adds a sentence explaining what the ring meant, drawn from verse 12 and 8:8.

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר הַמֶּ֨לֶךְ֙ לְהָמָ֔ן הַכֶּ֖סֶף נָת֣וּן לָ֑ךְ וְהָעָ֕ם לַעֲשׂ֥וֹת בּ֖וֹ כַּטּ֥וֹב בְּעֵינֶֽיךָ׃
records.gloss: And said the king to Haman, The silver [is] given to you, and the people, to do with it as the good in your eyes.
pieces: The king said to Haman, "The silver is yours, and the people too. Do with them as you see fit."

L.11: And the king said to Haman, "The silver is given to you, and the people also, to do with it as is good in your eyes."

R.11: The king said to Haman, "Keep the money, and do what you like with those people."

decisions.choice: the silver is given to you: probably the king lets Haman keep his money, or hands it back to him to use
alternatives: the king accepts the money and puts it at Haman's disposal
decisions.reason: The words can mean that the king refuses the payment out of royal generosity, or simply that he leaves the money matter in Haman's hands. Later Mordecai speaks of "the silver that Haman had promised to pay" (4:7), and Esther says "we have been sold" (7:4), which suggests the offer still stood. The text does not settle it.

decisions.choice: and the people, to do with it as you see fit
decisions.reason: The king hands over a whole people without asking who they are (see verse 8). The phrase "as is good in your eyes" gives Haman a free hand.

decisions.choice: Keep the money
alternatives: The silver is given to you
decisions.reason: Readable follows the more likely sense, that the king lets Haman keep it; the decision above gives the other reading.

records.source: וַיִּקָּרְאוּ֩ סֹפְרֵ֨י הַמֶּ֜לֶךְ בַּחֹ֣דֶשׁ הָרִאשׁ֗וֹן בִּשְׁלוֹשָׁ֨ה עָשָׂ֣ר יוֹם֮ בּוֹ֒ וַיִּכָּתֵ֣ב כְּֽכָל־אֲשֶׁר־צִוָּ֣ה הָמָ֡ן אֶ֣ל אֲחַשְׁדַּרְפְּנֵֽי־הַ֠מֶּלֶךְ וְֽאֶל־הַפַּח֞וֹת אֲשֶׁ֣ר׀עַל־מְדִינָ֣ה וּמְדִינָ֗ה וְאֶל־שָׂ֤רֵי עַם֙ וָעָ֔ם מְדִינָ֤ה וּמְדִינָה֙ כִּכְתָבָ֔הּ וְעַ֥ם וָעָ֖ם כִּלְשׁוֹנ֑וֹ בְּשֵׁ֨ם הַמֶּ֤לֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵרֹשׁ֙ נִכְתָּ֔ב וְנֶחְתָּ֖ם בְּטַבַּ֥עַת הַמֶּֽלֶךְ׃
records.gloss: And were summoned [the] scribes of the king in the month the first, on [the] thirteenth day in it, and it was written according to all that commanded Haman to [the] satraps of the king and to the governors who [were] over province and province and to [the] princes of people and people, province and province according to its script, and people and people according to its language; in [the] name of the king Ahasuerus [it was] written and sealed with the signet ring of the king.
pieces: The king's scribes were summoned on the thirteenth day of the first month, and a decree was written just as Haman commanded. It went to the king's satraps, to the governors over each province, and to the officials of each people, to every province in its own script and every people in its own language. It was written in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed with the king's signet ring.

L.12: And the scribes of the king were summoned in the first month, on the thirteenth day of it, and it was written according to all that Haman commanded to the satraps of the king and to the governors who were over each province and to the princes of each people, to each province in its own script and to each people in its own language. In the name of King Ahasuerus it was written, and it was sealed with the signet ring of the king.

R.12: On the thirteenth day of the first month, the king's secretaries were called in. They wrote down everything Haman ordered. The orders went to the king's regional governors, to the governors of each province, and to the leaders of each people group. Each province got the letter in its own kind of writing, and each people in its own language. The letters were written in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed with the king's signet ring.

decisions.choice: the thirteenth day of the first month: the day before Passover
decisions.reason: Passover fell on the fourteenth day of the first month (Exodus 12:6; Leviticus 23:5). The decree to destroy the Jews goes out on the eve of the feast that remembers their rescue from Egypt. The text does not point this out.

decisions.choice: satraps, governors and princes: the ranks of Persian government
decisions.reason: Satraps ruled the great regions of the empire, governors ruled provinces within them, and the princes were the leaders of the various peoples. The decree reaches every level, as the king's earlier letter did (1:22; 8:9).

decisions.choice: to each province in its script and each people in its language
decisions.reason: The Persian empire used many languages and writing systems; royal letters were translated for each region (1:22; 8:9). The thoroughness of the system now serves Haman's plan.

decisions.choice: regional governors
decisions.reason: Literal and Balanced keep the Persian title "satraps"; Readable says what they were.

decisions.choice: princes (Literal); officials (Balanced); leaders (Readable)
decisions.reason: As in verse 1, the word for a high officer follows the project's usual pattern.

records.source: וְנִשְׁל֨וֹחַ סְפָרִ֜ים בְּיַ֣ד הָרָצִים֮ אֶל־כָּל־מְדִינ֣וֹת הַמֶּלֶךְ֒ לְהַשְׁמִ֡יד לַהֲרֹ֣ג וּלְאַבֵּ֣ד אֶת־כָּל־הַ֠יְּהוּדִים מִנַּ֨עַר וְעַד־זָקֵ֜ן טַ֤ף וְנָשִׁים֙ בְּי֣וֹם אֶחָ֔ד בִּשְׁלוֹשָׁ֥ה עָשָׂ֛ר לְחֹ֥דֶשׁ שְׁנֵים־עָשָׂ֖ר הוּא־חֹ֣דֶשׁ אֲדָ֑ר וּשְׁלָלָ֖ם לָבֽוֹז׃
records.gloss: And were sent documents by [the] hand of the runners to all [the] provinces of the king, to annihilate, to kill and to destroy all the Jews, from young man and to old man, little ones and women, on day one, on [the] thirteenth of [the] month twelve, that [is the] month [of] Adar, and their spoil to plunder.
pieces: Letters were sent by couriers to all the king's provinces, ordering that all the Jews be wiped out, killed and destroyed, young and old, children and women, on a single day, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month Adar, and that their goods be taken as plunder.

L.13: And letters were sent by the hand of the runners to all the provinces of the king, to annihilate, to kill and to destroy all the Jews, from young man to old man, little ones and women, on one day, on the thirteenth of the twelfth month, which is the month Adar, and to plunder their spoil.

R.13: Messengers took the letters to all the king's provinces. The letters ordered that all the Jews be killed, every one of them, young and old, children and women. This was to happen on one day, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, the month of Adar. Their property could be taken.

decisions.choice: annihilate, kill and destroy: three verbs for total destruction
decisions.reason: The decree piles up three verbs, in legal style, to leave no doubt. Esther repeats them (7:4), and the counter-decree turns them around (8:11).

decisions.choice: from young man to old man, little ones and women: everyone, without exception
decisions.reason: The phrase lists the whole community, of every age and both sexes.

decisions.choice: the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, Adar: eleven months after the decree
decisions.reason: The decree went out in the first month (verse 12), so the Jews have almost a year of waiting. The day set by the lot (verse 7) becomes the day of reversal in 9:1.

decisions.choice: runners (Literal); couriers (Balanced); messengers (Readable)
decisions.reason: The "runners" were the royal mounted couriers of the Persian postal system (8:10, 14); Literal keeps the Hebrew word.

records.source: פַּתְשֶׁ֣גֶן הַכְּתָ֗ב לְהִנָּ֤תֵֽן דָּת֙ בְּכָל־מְדִינָ֣ה וּמְדִינָ֔ה גָּל֖וּי לְכָל־הָֽעַמִּ֑ים לִהְי֥וֹת עֲתִדִ֖ים לַיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּֽה׃
records.gloss: [The] copy of the writing, to be given [as] law in every province and province, [was] displayed to all the peoples, to be ready for the day the this.
pieces: A copy of the text was to be issued as law in every province and published to all the peoples, so that they would be ready for that day.

L.14: A copy of the writing was to be given as law in every province, made known to all the peoples, so that they would be ready for this day.

R.14: A copy of the order was to be made law in every province and announced to all the people, so that they would be ready for that day.

decisions.choice: copy: an official copy of a document
decisions.reason: The word is a Persian loanword for a written copy (4:8; 8:13; Ezra 4:11). The original was sealed in Susa; copies went out to be posted.

decisions.choice: to be given as law: to be issued as a royal decree with the force of law
decisions.reason: The word "law" here is the Persian word for a royal decree; such a law could not be revoked (1:19; 8:8).

decisions.choice: to be ready for this day: the peoples are to prepare for the appointed day
decisions.reason: The subject is the peoples of the empire, who are to be ready to carry out the decree on the thirteenth of Adar. The same words return in 8:13, where the Jews are to be ready to defend themselves.

decisions.choice: that day
decisions.reason: In English the day still to come reads more naturally as "that day"; Literal keeps "this".

records.source: הָֽרָצִ֞ים יָצְא֤וּ דְחוּפִים֙ בִּדְבַ֣ר הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ וְהַדָּ֥ת נִתְּנָ֖ה בְּשׁוּשַׁ֣ן הַבִּירָ֑ה וְהַמֶּ֤לֶךְ וְהָמָן֙ יָשְׁב֣וּ לִשְׁתּ֔וֹת וְהָעִ֥יר שׁוּשָׁ֖ן נָבֽוֹכָה׃פ
records.gloss: The runners went out hurried by [the] word of the king, and the law was given in Susa the citadel; and the king and Haman sat down to drink, and the city [of] Susa was in confusion.
pieces: At the king's command the couriers went out in haste, and the law was issued in the citadel of Susa. The king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was thrown into confusion.

L.15: The runners went out, hurried by the word of the king, and the law was given in Susa the citadel. And the king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was in confusion.

R.15: The messengers hurried out with the king's order, and the law was announced in the royal fortress in Susa. Then the king and Haman sat down to drink. But the people of the city of Susa were confused and upset.

decisions.choice: Susa the citadel: the fortified royal quarter of Susa, distinct from the city
decisions.reason: The book distinguishes the citadel, the palace fortress where the court lived (1:2), from the city of Susa around it. Here the law is made public in the citadel, and the city outside reacts.

decisions.choice: in confusion: bewildered, thrown into turmoil
decisions.reason: The verb is used of being perplexed and agitated (Exodus 14:3; Joel 1:18). The people of Susa, Jews and others, are shaken by the decree, while the king and Haman drink. The contrast is reversed in 8:15, when the city rejoices.

decisions.choice: the king and Haman sat down to drink
decisions.reason: Feasting and drinking run through the book (chapters 1, 2, 5, 7, 9). Here the two men who have doomed a people sit down to drink as if nothing had happened.

decisions.choice: the people of the city of Susa were confused and upset
decisions.reason: Readable says that the people of the city were troubled, which is what "the city was in confusion" means.
